A higher local CPI index does not establish which city costs more: keep the price anchors

Use two invented locations to separate price change over time from price differences across places, then compare after-tax income, matched spending and upfront moving cash.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Separate two local time indexes from independently anchored household price quotes

Interactive planning lab

Current matched-bundle cash cost in A$54,000
Current matched-bundle cash cost in B$66,000
Annual cash left: B minus A$3,000
Cumulative B-minus-A cash difference after moving cost$7,000

Original hypothetical two-location example, with no actual city names, published CPI observations or live price quotes. The same quantities and quality of a modeled annual spending bundle are assumed in both locations and both periods. Each location’s own baseline cost is independently set to index 100. A current local time index equals current bundle cost divided by that location’s baseline cost, multiplied by 100. It measures change within that location; the missing cross-location price anchor cannot be recovered from the two time indexes alone. This simple fixed-bundle illustration does not reproduce official CPI basket updates, sampling or quality adjustments. The two quoted baseline costs are separate assumptions, rather than prices inferred from a CPI comparison. After obtaining current costs, the cash scenario holds them and the independently entered after-tax annual incomes constant for all completed future years. It does not apply the current index repeatedly as an annual inflation forecast. Moving cost is paid at time zero; the annual cash advantage arrives at each year-end. The cumulative line shows only the incremental B-minus-A cash difference, with no opening bank balance, financing, interest or affordability assessment. Negative annual amounts and negative cumulative differences remain visible. The bundle covers only the stated modeled recurring spending; a real comparison needs complete actual budgets, route and housing comparability, commitments, income reliability and separately available upfront cash. No tax calculation, benefit estimate, property purchase, return, borrowing or recommendation to relocate is supplied.

The central idea

A time index normalizes each location’s starting price. Comparing the index numbers alone cannot recover the dollar price difference that was normalized away.

01

Separate a change over time from a comparison across places

Suppose a local price index is 120 in location A and 110 in location B, with each location’s own baseline set to 100. It is tempting to conclude that A is the more expensive place. Those two time-index numbers alone do not establish that conclusion.

Statistics Canada’s CPI FAQ explains that the CPI measures price change through time and that its index-reference value is assigned to 100. A time index describes a price relative to its own reference, rather than quoting a basket in dollars.

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI FAQ explicitly distinguishes local price change from differences in price levels between areas. This article uses that measurement principle without importing U.S. price data or applying U.S. rules.

The example below is entirely invented. A and B are unnamed locations, and the simple fixed-bundle indexes do not reproduce every feature of an official CPI program.

02

Give each location an independent dollar anchor

Assume the same annual quantities and quality of a spending bundle originally cost CAD 45,000 in A and CAD 60,000 in B. Set each local baseline cost to index 100.

The equal index values conceal an original dollar difference. They mean each location is being compared with itself at the baseline date. They do not mean that CAD 45,000 and CAD 60,000 are the same price.

Now set A’s current index to 120 and B’s to 110. A’s modeled cost is CAD 45,000 × 120 ÷ 100 = CAD 54,000. B’s is CAD 60,000 × 110 ÷ 100 = CAD 66,000.

A has experienced the larger proportional increase from its own starting point, yet B still has the higher current dollar cost. The first pair of charts keeps both views visible: locally normalized time indexes and the independently anchored cash amounts.

03

Use the right denominator for the question

For the within-location change, A’s current cost divided by its own baseline is 1.2, a 20% increase. B’s corresponding ratio is 1.1, a 10% increase. Those calculations answer how each location changed.

For the modeled current spatial comparison, divide B’s CAD 66,000 cost by A’s CAD 54,000 cost. The result is about 1.2222, meaning B’s matched bundle costs about 22.2% more than A’s at the comparison date.

Dividing the two time-index values, 120 ÷ 110, does not produce that price ratio. It omits the original CAD 45,000 and CAD 60,000 anchors. The direction of the index comparison can therefore differ from the direction of the dollar comparison.

Try changing the baseline quotes while leaving both current index values unchanged. The first chart stays the same, while the dollar costs can change and even reverse their ordering. That is a direct demonstration of the information the time indexes alone do not contain.

04

Changing the reference value does not change the prices

If both local series were instead rebased to the current period, both current index values would be 100 again. The current cash costs would remain CAD 54,000 and CAD 66,000. A normalization convention does not make the underlying prices converge.

For A, the old baseline would then appear at about 83.33, calculated as 100 ÷ 1.2. For B, it would appear at about 90.91, calculated as 100 ÷ 1.1. The within-series proportional changes remain the same after consistent rebasing.

The example also assumes a genuinely matched bundle across locations: the same quantities and quality. Real housing, transport access, household needs and service levels can differ. Similar category labels do not establish that two quoted budgets buy an equivalent standard of living.

Statistics Canada distinguishes a fixed-basket price index from a complete cost-of-living measure. This article does not price well-being, public services, family support or other features of a location that can matter to a household.

05

Bring income and the actual spending comparison into the budget

The independent income assumptions are CAD 70,000 of annual after-tax cash in A and CAD 85,000 in B. Subtracting the modeled current bundle costs leaves CAD 16,000 in A and CAD 19,000 in B.

B’s additional net income is CAD 15,000, while its additional bundle cost is CAD 12,000. The annual B-minus-A cash difference is therefore CAD 3,000. The waterfall separates those two contributions.

This is a cash-budget comparison under the entered assumptions. It does not follow directly from either price index. The incomes are already after tax, so the model does not deduct income tax a second time.

A real comparison needs complete personal budgets. If the modeled bundle omits a payment that differs between locations, the CAD 3,000 difference is incomplete. Check housing terms, commuting, care, debt and other commitments rather than treating the residual as automatically available for a new goal.

06

Place the moving cost before the annual advantage

The example assumes CAD 8,000 of moving cash paid at time zero. The cumulative incremental cash line therefore begins at negative CAD 8,000 relative to remaining in A.

Each completed year then adds the assumed CAD 3,000 annual cash advantage. The differences are negative CAD 5,000 after year one, negative CAD 2,000 after year two and positive CAD 1,000 after year three. After five completed years, the difference is positive CAD 7,000.

The line shows only the difference between the alternatives. It is not an account balance, and a negative starting difference does not mean the model has arranged an overdraft. The moving cash must be available separately at the time it is paid.

If B has no annual cash advantage, a positive moving cost is not recovered in this simple comparison. If B has a recurring disadvantage, the difference becomes more negative. The chart keeps those outcomes visible instead of assuming that every move has a payback date.

07

Do not turn the current index into an unexamined future forecast

The current index of 120 represents a change from the chosen baseline. It does not mean prices rise by 20% every future year. The cash-calendar panel holds the resulting current costs and the entered incomes constant to isolate the moving-cost comparison.

Future inflation, income growth, changes in employment, financing and investment returns are outside this model. If those assumptions matter, create dated scenarios for both alternatives rather than repeatedly applying one observed index number.

For an actual relocation decision, obtain current comparable quotes and verify the income that would be received after tax. Budget deposits, overlapping housing, transport, setup expenses and any other upfront payments at their dates.

Use a time index to understand change within its stated scope. Use matched current prices and a complete cash calendar to compare the household alternatives. Keeping both pieces inspectable prevents a convenient normalized number from replacing the financial evidence the decision requires.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Four original hypothetical charts use two matched spending bundles and independent price anchors. No published CPI value, actual city quote, cost-of-living ranking or relocation recommendation is shown. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
